question: A story's acceptance criterion reads: "The backend caches the result in Redis for 60 seconds." It is binary and mechanically verifiable — yet it is flagged as an anti-pattern. What is the defect?
choices: It is not measurable enough: the criterion should also pin the Redis eviction policy and memory ceiling to be fully testable
Caching concerns are non-functional, so the statement belongs in the team's Definition of Done rather than in story-level AC

It specifies how instead of what: an AC is a contract on observable behavior, so it should state the user-visible guarantee — e.g. repeated identical searches within 60 seconds return consistent results in under 50 ms — and leave the mechanism to design docs
The format is wrong: a caching rule involves a trigger and an outcome, so it must be rewritten as a Given/When/Then scenario to be automatable
explanation: AC describe what the system does from the outside — what a tester, PO, or customer would recognize as "the thing working" — never how it is built. "Caches in Redis for 60s" welds the story to one design: it cannot be verified without inspecting internals, it forbids equally valid implementations (in-process cache, CDN, precomputation), and it silently goes stale the day the design changes. Restated as an observable guarantee — a consistency window plus a latency threshold — the criterion survives any implementation and stays testable at the system boundary. Pinning eviction policy digs even deeper into implementation; the DoD holds team-wide gates that apply to every story, not story-specific behavior; and checklist-vs-Gherkin is orthogonal — the defect is the content, not the format.

question: A story specifies shipping-fee calculation: the fee depends on cart-value bands (under €50, €50–100, over €100), destination zone (domestic, EU, non-EU), and a free-shipping promo flag. The author writes 14 Gherkin scenarios that are word-for-word identical except for those three inputs and the expected fee. Review flags the AC as unmaintainable. What does the format guidance prescribe?
choices: Downgrade to a rule-oriented checklist — one bullet per combination ('domestic order under €50 ships for €4.90', …) — since bullets carry the same information with far less Gherkin ceremony

Apply the count smell: fourteen criteria is triple the healthy limit, so the story is several stories in disguise — split it into one story per destination zone, each carrying its own handful of scenarios

This is the calculations row of the format table: Gherkin with a Scenario Outline. One template captures the single behaviour — a fee computed from cart value, zone, and promo — and the equivalence classes move into the Examples table, one row per class with the band boundaries included. The 14 copies bury the rule: nobody can see the banding structure through the repetition, and any wording fix must land 14 times, which is how drift starts. The Outline preserves exactly what Gherkin was chosen for — explicit context, single trigger, observable outcome — while making the variation what it truly is: data, not behaviour. One discipline carries over: keep the Examples to the classes and boundaries that change the outcome, because Outline overuse (data sweeps, especially through the UI) is its own anti-pattern

Keep the 14 scenarios: each is independently testable with its own pass/fail verdict, and in specifications explicitness beats deduplication — a reader should never have to mentally substitute table values to know what is asserted
explanation: The reviewer's instinct is right and the format table names the cure: calculations, pricing, and rules-engine logic are exactly where Scenario Outline earns its place, because the thing being specified is one behaviour applied across equivalence classes of inputs. The 14-copy version fails as specification before it fails as maintenance: a specification's job is to make the rule visible, and the banding structure — three value bands × three zones, modulated by a promo flag — is invisible when smeared across fourteen near-identical blocks but legible at a glance as an Examples table whose rows are the classes and boundaries. The maintenance cost follows: identical wording duplicated 14 times drifts the first time someone fixes one copy. The distractors each misapply a real guideline. The checklist format is for static, trigger-less assertions (layout, copy, compliance thresholds); conditional logic with a trigger and an observable outcome is what Given/When/Then exists to structure, and bullets would just re-encode the same 14 rows minus that structure. The >5-AC count smell signals multiple behaviours hiding in one story — but here there is exactly one behaviour with many data rows, so splitting by zone would manufacture three anaemic stories that can't ship independently and still each need an Examples table. And the explicitness defense dissolves on inspection: each Examples row runs as its own scenario with its own pass/fail verdict, so independent testability is fully preserved — the Outline removes duplication of the behaviour text, not the concreteness of the data.
